title: Bob Wasn't Loyal, He Was Trapped
author: bytitleonly
summary: The newsletter uses the story of 'Bob,' a 38-year IBM employee celebrated at his retirement party as a model of loyalty, to expose what loyalty myths in organizations actually look like. Bob did not stay for 38 years because IBM was a great place or because he was deeply committed to the mission. He stayed because of pension vesting cliffs, health insurance lock-in, a mortgage adjusted to his salary, and the sunk-cost psychology of 'I've been here 20 years, I might as well stay for 40.' The piece argues that what organizations call loyalty is almost always forced compliance: structural golden handcuffs that make leaving too costly to contemplate. The real cost is human: Bob spent his career in a state of resigned endurance rather than genuine engagement, and the organization received compliance rather than the energy of someone who chose to be there. The piece closes with a leadership charge: build organizations people stay in because they want to, not because they can't afford to leave.
points: * Bob's 38-year tenure at IBM was not loyalty but forced compliance: pension cliffs, health insurance lock-in, and sunk-cost psychology made leaving more costly than staying, regardless of engagement or meaning. * Organizations that celebrate long tenure as evidence of loyalty are celebrating the effectiveness of their golden handcuffs, not the quality of their culture or the commitment of their people. * The real cost of structural lock-in is not financial but human: employees in golden handcuffs deliver compliance, not the discretionary energy of someone who has chosen to be there. * The distinction between loyalty and entrapment matters for leadership because the interventions are opposite: entrapment requires removing the handcuffs, while genuine loyalty requires building something worth choosing. * The piece makes a specific diagnostic claim: you can tell the difference between loyalty and entrapment by asking 'would this person stay if the pension reset tomorrow?' If the honest answer is no, you have entrapment, not loyalty.
quotes: At Bob's retirement party, his manager called him 'one of the most loyal employees IBM has ever had.' Bob smiled. His wife smiled. Everyone applauded. And I thought: loyal to what, exactly? To a company that restructured his division three times? To work he described, when I asked him privately, as 'fine, I guess'?

Bob stayed for 38 years because leaving at year 15 would have cost him his pension. Because his health insurance was IBM's. Because his mortgage was sized to his IBM salary. Because at year 20 he started telling himself 'might as well stay for 40.'

What organizations call loyalty is almost always structural capture. The golden handcuffs are effective. The pension cliff works. The health insurance lock-in works. What they produce is compliant bodies, not engaged minds.

The loyal employee shows up differently than the trapped one. They bring an idea on Tuesday afternoon not because they have to, not because it's in their KPIs, but because they give a damn. You can feel the difference in a room.
Build something people stay in because they want to, not because they can't afford to leave. The loyalty you earn that way is the only kind worth having.
